subject: ela
description: Students analyze how a particular part of a literary text (a sentence, paragraph, chapter, scene, or stanza) fits into the overall structure of the whole and how that part contributes to the development of the theme, setting, or plot. They identify where a part sits in the arc of a story, poem, or play; explain the job that part does (such as introducing a conflict, shifting the setting, building tension, marking a turning point, or resolving an action); and connect a structural choice by the author to its effect on meaning. Every item embeds the full passage, excerpt, stanza, or scene it depends on, so the student needs nothing external.
subSkills: Identify the part being analyzed and locate it within the whole (beginning, middle, climax, falling action, resolution; opening or closing stanza; first or final scene)

Name the structural job a sentence, paragraph, chapter, scene, or stanza does (introduce a character or setting, raise a conflict, build suspense, mark a turning point, reveal a change, resolve the plot)
Explain how a specific part advances the plot, by linking it to what came before and what it sets up next
Explain how a specific part develops the setting, by showing how it establishes or shifts time, place, or mood
Explain how a specific part develops the theme, by connecting it to the lesson, message, or central idea of the text
Recognize structural features of different genres (chapters and scenes in prose and drama; stanzas, lines, and refrains in poetry) and how the author orders them
Evaluate why the author placed a part where they did and how moving or removing it would change the reader's understanding

problemArchetypes.name: Locate the part in the overall structure
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short excerpt. Where does this moment fall in the structure of the story, and how do you know? Answer: It is the climax, the highest point of tension, because the main character finally faces the problem that has been building since the opening.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the structural job of a part
problemArchetypes.example: Read the opening paragraph. What does this paragraph do for the story as a whole? Answer: It introduces the setting and the main character's ordinary world so that the later change feels dramatic.

problemArchetypes.name: Connect a part to plot development
problemArchetypes.example: Read the scene. How does this scene move the plot forward? Answer: It introduces the conflict between the two friends, which sets up the argument that drives the rest of the story.

problemArchetypes.name: Connect a part to setting development
problemArchetypes.example: Read the stanza. How does this stanza develop the setting of the poem? Answer: It shifts the time from day to night and creates a lonely, cold mood that makes the speaker's feelings clear.

problemArchetypes.name: Connect a part to theme development
problemArchetypes.example: Read the final chapter excerpt. How does this ending contribute to the theme of the text? Answer: By showing the character forgive her sister, the ending develops the theme that family bonds matter more than being right.

problemArchetypes.name: Evaluate the effect of structural placement
problemArchetypes.example: Read the excerpt. Why might the author have placed this flashback in the middle of the story instead of at the beginning? Answer: Placing it in the middle delays the reveal so the reader feels the same surprise the character does, deepening the emotional effect.

Easy.description: A short, clearly structured stimulus (a single stanza, one paragraph, or a brief 3 to 6 line scene, roughly 40 to 80 words) embedded in the item. The structure is obvious and the relationship is stated or strongly signaled in the text. The task is to identify where the part sits or name the simple job it does, with one structural concept tested and little inference required.
constraints: Stimulus is one short paragraph, one stanza, or a brief scene of roughly 40 to 80 words included in the prompt
Tests one concept: locate the part (beginning, middle, end) or name an obvious job (introduce setting, introduce character)
Identify-level task with explicit textual signals
The connection to plot, setting, or theme is direct and stated, requiring minimal inference

Medium.description: A moderate stimulus (a longer paragraph, a two or three stanza poem section, or a short scene, roughly 90 to 160 words) embedded in the item, with a less obvious structure. The task requires analysis: explaining how a specified part contributes to the development of the plot, setting, or theme by linking it to other parts of the text. The student must reason about cause and effect within the structure, not just label a part.
constraints: Stimulus is a longer paragraph, multi-stanza excerpt, or short scene of roughly 90 to 160 words in the prompt
Tests how a part develops plot, setting, or theme, with the connection implied rather than stated
Analyze-level task: explain the part's contribution by relating it to what comes before or after
Distractors are plausible but confuse the part's job (for example, calling a rising action moment the resolution)

Hard.description: A complex multi-part stimulus (a passage with two contrasting sections, a full short scene, or a complete short poem, roughly 170 to 260 words) embedded in the item. The task requires evaluation: judging why the author structured the text as they did, comparing the function of two parts, or explaining how a structural choice (placement, ordering, a shift, a refrain) shapes the development of theme, setting, or plot. Requires inference about authorial intent and effect on the reader.
constraints: Stimulus is a passage with contrasting sections, a complete short scene, or a full short poem of roughly 170 to 260 words in the prompt
Tests the effect of a structural choice (ordering, placement, shift, repetition) or compares the roles of two parts
Evaluate-level task: justify why the structure works or how a change would alter meaning
Requires inference about authorial intent and the effect on the reader; distractors reflect partial or surface readings

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student summarizes what the part says instead of explaining what the part does for the overall structure
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Answers by retelling the events of the excerpt rather than identifying its structural job (such as introducing the conflict or marking the turning point)

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student misjudges where the part falls in the arc, confusing rising action with the climax or resolution
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Labels a tension-building moment as the resolution, or calls the opening setup the climax, ignoring that the conflict has not yet peaked

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student connects the part to the wrong story element, crediting it with developing plot when it develops setting, or theme when it develops plot
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Says a descriptive stanza advances the plot when it actually establishes the setting and mood, or says an action scene reveals the theme when it mainly moves the plot

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats each chapter, scene, or stanza as a standalone unit and fails to relate the part to the whole text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Explains the part only on its own terms, never linking it to what came before or what it sets up next

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses a poem's stanzas or a play's scenes with prose chapters and applies the wrong structural vocabulary
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Describes a stanza as a chapter or a scene as a stanza, mislabeling the genre's structural units

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes the part's placement is arbitrary and cannot explain why the author put it where it is
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims the order does not matter or that the part could appear anywhere, ignoring how placement builds suspense, delays a reveal, or shapes the theme

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student identifies a theme that the text does not actually support and forces the part to fit it
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Connects the part to a generic or unsupported moral instead of the central idea the passage actually develops
